name: Words trivia (hard)
description: 50 hard questions about word meanings, origins, spelling, idioms, grammar. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: The word 'petrichor', coined in 1964 for the smell of rain on dry earth, joins the Greek for 'stone' with 'ichor'. In Greek myth, what is ichor?
answers: The fluid in the veins of the gods
The nectar drunk at divine feasts
The mist rising from the river Styx
The dust shaken from Hermes' sandals
items.correct: The fluid in the veins of the gods
items.explain: Petrichor was coined from Greek petros (stone) plus ichor, the fluid that supposedly flows in the veins of the gods.

items.question: In which scientific journal did Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Grenfell Thomas publish the 1964 article that coined 'petrichor'?
items.explain: Their article 'Nature of Argillaceous Odour' appeared in the journal Nature in 1964 and introduced the word petrichor.

items.question: What error created the ghost word 'dord', which appeared in Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition (1934)?
answers: A typesetter's mistranscription of the word 'dorm'
A joke entry added by an editor and left in
An abbreviation slip 'D or d' read as one word
A scientist's coinage filed in the main list
items.correct: An abbreviation slip 'D or d' read as one word
items.explain: A 1931 slip gave 'D or d' as abbreviations for density. Because of how such slips were spaced, it was misread as a single word, 'dord', meaning density.

source.title: How a Ghost Word Appeared in the Dictionary (Video)

items.question: Which Victorian philologist coined the term 'ghost word' for words that have no real existence?
items.explain: The philologist Skeat coined 'ghost word', saying such words are like ghosts: we may seem to see them, but they have no real entity.

items.question: Horace Walpole coined 'serendipity' in a letter dated 28 January 1754. To which friend was it addressed?
items.explain: Walpole explained the new word in a letter to his friend Sir Horace Mann, while describing a discovery about a painting.

items.question: 'Serendip', the old name for Sri Lanka behind 'serendipity', comes via Arabic from the Sanskrit 'Simhaladvipa'. What does that mean?
items.explain: Serendip comes from Arabic Sarandib, from Sanskrit Simhaladvipa, glossed as 'Dwelling-Place-of-Lions Island'.

items.question: Which American writer coined the word 'mondegreen' in a 1954 Harper's Magazine column?
items.explain: Sylvia Wright coined the word in her column 'The Death of Lady Mondegreen', based on her childhood mishearing of a Scottish ballad.

items.question: What is the Greek-derived term for a word or phrase that appears only once in a given text or body of literature?
items.explain: Hapax legomenon comes from Greek words for 'once' and 'being said', and names a word that occurs once in a corpus.

items.question: The term 'hapax legomenon' was created by Hellenistic scholars in Alexandria who were studying which works?
answers: Hesiod's Theogony and Works and Days
items.explain: The term was created by the Homeric scholars in Alexandria during the Hellenistic Age as they studied the Iliad and the Odyssey.

source.title: Hapax Legomena: Ten Biblical Examples - TheTorah.com

items.question: Which law of word frequency predicts that hapax legomena (words occurring once) are very common in any large body of text?
items.explain: Zipf's law says a word's frequency is inversely related to its rank, so many words occur only once. In large corpora roughly 40 to 60 percent of word types are hapax legomena.

items.question: What is the linguistic term for inserting a word into the middle of another word, as in 'abso-bloody-lutely'?
items.explain: Tmesis is the use of a word or words in the middle of another word. The term comes from Greek tmesis, meaning 'a cutting'.

source.title: tmesis noun - Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary

items.question: Which playwright created Mrs Malaprop, who gave her name to 'malapropism', in the 1775 comedy The Rivals?
items.explain: Mrs Malaprop appears in Sheridan's The Rivals (1775). The term malapropism derives from her habit of swapping similar-sounding words.

items.question: Mrs Malaprop's name is taken from the French 'mal à propos'. What does that phrase mean?
items.explain: Malapropism is named after Mrs Malaprop, whose name comes from the French mal à propos, meaning 'inappropriate'.

items.question: The linguistic term 'eggcorn' is itself an eggcorn, an altered form of which word?
items.explain: The term comes from a case where 'acorn' was rendered as 'egg corn'. That is why the word is itself an example of what it names.

items.question: Which linguist coined the term 'eggcorn' in 2003?
items.explain: Linguist Geoffrey Pullum proposed the term in 2003 after a Language Log post about a woman who wrote 'egg corns' for 'acorns'.

items.question: The 'Jerusalem' in 'Jerusalem artichoke' is often cited as a folk etymology of an Italian word. What does that word, 'girasole', mean?
items.explain: 'Jerusalem' is thought to be a reshaping of Italian girasole, 'sunflower'. The Jerusalem artichoke is a kind of sunflower.

items.question: Which bird-themed folk-etymology form is given as a classic case of people reshaping 'asparagus' into something more familiar?
items.explain: Asparagus was reanalysed as 'sparrow-grass', which sounded more familiar to listeners who did not know the original word.

items.question: In the word 'interrobang', the 'bang' part comes from the typesetters' name for which mark?
items.explain: Martin Speckter named the mark from 'interro' (interrogation point) and 'bang', typesetters' slang for the exclamation mark.

source.title: INTERROBANG—YOU CALL THAT A HAT?! - Word of the Week

items.question: In 1966 American Type Founders issued a metal typeface that included the interrobang. What was it called?
items.explain: American Type Founders' 1966 metal typeface Americana was among the first to include the interrobang, which Martin Speckter proposed in 1962.

source.title: Interrobang: The Punctuation Mark Invented in 1962

items.question: Which Roman poet's warning against 'words a foot and a half long' gave English the word 'sesquipedalian'?
items.explain: Horace used the Latin phrase sesquipedalia verba ('words a foot and a half long') in his Ars Poetica, and 'sesquipedalian' derives from it.

items.question: What choice did Thomas Hobson, the Cambridge stable owner behind the phrase 'Hobson's choice', give his customers?
answers: Take any horse but pay double
Take the oldest horse or wait a week
Take a horse unridden for a month
Take the horse nearest the door or none
items.correct: Take the horse nearest the door or none
items.explain: Hobson offered the horse in the stall nearest the door or no horse at all, so the phrase means an apparent choice with only one real option.

items.question: Which poet helped make the Cambridge carrier Thomas Hobson, and the phrase 'Hobson's choice', well known through his mock epitaphs?
items.explain: Milton, a Cambridge student in the years before Hobson died in 1631, wrote comic epitaphs on him. Etymologists credit him with making the phrase popular.

source.title: Hobson's choice - Origin & Meaning of the Phrase

items.question: A common error replaces 'Hobson's choice' with a phrase that confuses Thomas Hobson with a philosopher. What is the erroneous phrase?
items.explain: People sometimes say 'Hobbesian choice', confusing the philosopher Thomas Hobbes with the relatively obscure Thomas Hobson.

items.question: 'Quarantine' derives from the Italian 'quaranta giorni'. For how many days were ships from infected ports made to sit at anchor off Venice?
items.explain: Ships arriving in Venice from infected ports had to wait at anchor for 40 days. 'Quaranta giorni' means 'forty days'.

items.question: The Latin 'salarium', ancestor of the English word 'salary', is linked to 'sal', the Latin word for what?
items.explain: 'Salary' comes from Latin salarium, 'pertaining to salt' (sal, 'salt'). The exact connection is unclear, and the claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is baseless.

items.question: 'Pedigree' comes from the Anglo-French 'pé de grue'. Literally, whose foot is that?
items.explain: Pé de grue means 'crane's foot'. The branching lines of a genealogical chart resembled the shape of a crane's foot.

items.question: The contronym 'cleave' can mean both 'to split' and 'to cling'. Why does it have two opposite meanings?
answers: One Latin verb whose sense was later reversed
A Norse loanword respelled by the Normans
Two separate Old English verbs that merged in form
A Greek root carrying two opposite prefixes
items.correct: Two separate Old English verbs that merged in form
items.explain: 'Cleave' comes from two different Old English words, clēofan and cleofian, which became identical in form.

source.title: Contronyms You've Been Using Without Realizing It

items.question: The contronym 'bound' can mean 'tied up' or 'ready to go', as in 'bound for Paris'. The 'ready' sense comes from which language's word 'būinn'?
items.explain: One sense of 'bound' comes from Old English bindan ('to bind'). The other comes from Old Norse būinn, 'to get ready'.

source.title: Contronyms You've Been Using Without Realizing It

items.question: Which alternative name for a word that is its own opposite refers to a two-faced Roman god?
items.explain: A contronym is also called a Janus word, after the Roman god Janus, who had two faces looking in opposite directions.

source.title: How to Use Contronym and auto-antonym Correctly

items.question: William Spooner, the Oxford don who gave his name to the 'spoonerism', reportedly claimed that his only genuine spoonerism involved what?
items.explain: Spooner himself said his sole real spoonerism was a garbled reference to a hymn. Most of the others were probably invented by colleagues and students.

items.question: Johannes Hofer coined 'nostalgia' in 1688 to describe the homesickness of which group?
answers: Crusader knights in the Holy Land
items.explain: Hofer coined 'nostalgia' from Greek 'nóstos' (homecoming) and 'álgos' (pain). He used it for the condition seen in Swiss mercenaries pining for their homeland.

items.question: Thomas Bowdler's name gave English the verb 'bowdlerize'. Who largely did the work on the first, anonymous 1807 edition of The Family Shakespeare?
items.explain: The 1807 edition appeared anonymously and was largely the work of Thomas Bowdler's sister, Henrietta Maria Bowdler. Her brother's name later became the eponym.

source.title: Bowdler Publishes The Family Shakespeare - EBSCO Research Starters

items.question: Karel Čapek popularized the word 'robot' in his play R.U.R. Whom did he always credit as the word's true originator?
items.explain: Karel Čapek had been toying with 'labori' for his artificial workers. His brother Josef, a painter, suggested 'roboti', and Karel always credited him with the coinage.

source.title: Where does the word 'robot' come from? - BBC Science Focus Magazine

items.question: In Hebrew, the word 'shibboleth' used as a test in Judges 12 literally refers to which part of a plant?
answers: The ear of a cereal stalk
items.correct: The ear of a cereal stalk
items.explain: Hebrew 'shibbōleth' means an ear of grain (or possibly a flowing stream). The English sense of a test-word comes from the Gileadites using it against fleeing Ephraimites.

items.question: Which artist drew the 1812 Boston Gazette cartoon 'The Gerry-mander', which helped fix the word 'gerrymander' in the public mind?
items.explain: Elkanah Tisdale's satirical cartoon turned a Massachusetts district into a salamander-like creature. It popularized the term derived from Governor Elbridge Gerry's name.

items.question: In which 1950 book does the word 'nerd' appear in print for the first known time, as the name of a creature?
items.explain: Dr. Seuss's 1950 book If I Ran the Zoo has the earliest known printed 'nerd'. The modern slang sense seems to have developed separately in the early 1950s.

source.title: The Many Origin Stories of 'Nerd' - Merriam-Webster

items.question: Which poet's challenge at a British Association meeting in 1833 led William Whewell to invent the word 'scientist'?
items.explain: Coleridge challenged the association over what its members should be called. Whewell proposed 'scientist', by analogy with 'artist'.

source.title: William Whewell - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

items.question: In Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost, which character speaks the long word 'honorificabilitudinitatibus'?
items.explain: The clown Costard says the word in Act V, Scene 1, teasing the small page Moth. It appears nowhere else in Shakespeare's works.

items.question: Ernest Vincent Wright's 1939 novel Gadsby, which avoids the letter E entirely, is an example of which constrained-writing form?
items.explain: A lipogram is a text that deliberately avoids one or more letters. Gadsby runs to over 50,000 words without an 'e'.

items.question: The 45-letter word 'pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis' was coined in 1935 by the president of which organization?
items.explain: Everett M. Smith, then president of the National Puzzlers' League, coined it at the group's meeting as a deliberately long word.

items.question: The ampersand (&) began as a ligature of which two letters in Roman cursive?
items.explain: The symbol comes from the Latin word 'et', meaning 'and', with the E and T joined together. The English name 'ampersand' is a later corruption of 'and per se and'.

items.question: J.R.R. Tolkien interpreted his surname as the Low German for 'dull-keen'. That is a literal equivalent of which Greek-derived English word?
items.explain: 'Oxymoron' joins Greek 'oxús' (sharp) and 'mōrós' (dull or foolish). Tolkien's reading of his surname as 'dull-keen' matches that structure.

items.question: In 'disaster', from Italian 'disastro' (literally 'ill-starred'), what does the prefix 'dis-' contribute?
answers: It adds a sense of 'ill' or 'bad'
It negates the star, meaning 'no star'
items.correct: It adds a sense of 'ill' or 'bad'
items.explain: Here 'dis-' is merely pejorative, like English 'mis-', so 'disastro' means 'ill-starred'. The sense is astrological, a calamity blamed on an unfavourable star.

items.question: In which century is the first known English use of 'defenestration' recorded?
items.explain: Merriam-Webster dates the first known use to 1619. That was just after the 1618 Defenestration of Prague, the event that gave the word its fame.

items.question: The English word 'robot' comes from the Czech 'robota'. What did 'robota' mean?
items.explain: Czech 'robota' meant forced labor, compulsory service or drudgery, from an Old Slavic root related to 'slave'. The word was popularized by R.U.R. in 1920.

items.question: Which of these words did William Whewell coin at the request of Michael Faraday?
items.explain: Whewell invented 'anode', 'cathode' and 'ion' for Faraday. 'Electron', 'photon' and 'proton' were coined by other people.

source.title: William Whewell - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

items.question: 'Honorificabilitudinitatibus' is said to be the longest English word with which distinctive letter pattern?
answers: No letter appearing more than once
items.explain: The 27-letter word alternates consonants and vowels throughout. It is described as the longest English word to do so.

items.question: At which university did Johannes Hofer present the 1688 dissertation that coined 'nostalgia'?
items.explain: Hofer coined the term in a dissertation at the University of Basel. He rendered the German 'Heimweh' (homesickness) into Greek-based Modern Latin.

items.question: In 1818 Thomas Bowdler published an expanded edition of The Family Shakspeare. How many plays did it cover?
items.explain: The 1807 first edition covered 20 plays. Bowdler's 1818 expansion covered all 36 plays then available, and gave us 'bowdlerize'.
